claim: Extinction training, in which the aversive outcome is omitted, leads to reduction in learned fear.
source: Tremendous progress has been made in this regard through extinction training in which the aversive outcome is omitted.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about extinction training in fear conditioning.

claim: The infralimbic cortex has a specific role in fear reduction that depends on the omission of aversive events but not on overexpectation.
source: We report that the infralimbic cortex has a very specific role in fear reduction that depends on the omission of aversive events but not on overexpectation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiment 1 showing IL inactivation disrupts extinction but not overexpectation.

claim: The orbitofrontal cortex is critical for downregulating fear when novel predictions about upcoming aversive events are generated.
source: The orbitofrontal cortex, a structure generally overlooked in fear, is critical for downregulating fear when novel predictions about upcoming aversive events are generated, such as when fear is inflated or overexpected, but less so when an expected aversive event is omitted.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from Experiments 2 and 3 showing lOFC inactivation disrupts overexpectation but has limited effect on extinction.

claim: Extinction involves the dramatic reduction in fear-related behaviours after presenting a previously established signal for an aversive event in the absence of that event.
source: In the context of fear learning, extinction involves the dramatic reduction in fear-related behaviours typically observed after presenting a previously established signal for an aversive event (i.e., a tone paired with shock; tone →shock) in the absence of that event (tone presented alone; tone → nothing).
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about extinction in fear conditioning.

claim: Extinction is effective in the treatment of anxiety disorders.
source: Given its simplicity and effectiveness in the treatment of anxiety disorders (Schiller et al., 2010; Milad and Quirk, 2012; Craske et al., 2018; Ebrahimi et al., 2020; Geller et al., 2019; Hammoud et al., 2020), extinction has received significant attention in a quest to understand its underlying behavioural and neural mechanisms (e.g., An et al., 2017; Morgan et al., 1993; Quirk et al., 2000; Milad and Quirk, 2002; Leung and Westbrook, 2008; Leung and Westbrook, 2010; Likhtik et al., 2008; Herry et al., 2008; Monfils et al., 2009 Johansen et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: In overexpectation, reduction in previously established fear responses occurs despite continued delivery of the aversive event.
source: In overexpectation, reduction in previously established fear responses ensue, strikingly, despite continued delivery of the aversive event.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the overexpectation phenomenon.

claim: Separately established signals of a common aversive event can summate their fear-inducing properties when encountered simultaneously.
source: This is possible because separately established signals of a common aversive event (i.e., tone → shock; light→shock) can summate their fear-inducing properties when encountered simultaneously (tone+light), triggering a state of exacerbated fear.
evidence: This is established knowledge about summation in fear conditioning.

claim: The presentation of an unintensified aversive event in a state of exacerbated fear engages a self-regulatory mechanism that lessens the exacerbated fear.
source: The presentation of the same (i.e., unintensified) aversive event in that state (tone+light →shock) engages a self-regulatory mechanism that lessens the exacerbated fear by partially extinguishing the fear elicited by each individual signal (Rescorla, 1970; Rescorla, 2006; Rescorla, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Rescorla's work on overexpectation.

claim: Failure to reduce fear by overexpectation is a likely contributor to aberrant and persistent fear characterizing anxiety disorders.
source: Since signals for threat often co-occur (think of the sight of a microphone and that of a staring crowd for a glossophobic), failure to reduce fear by overexpectation is a likely contributor to the aberrant and persistent fear characterizing anxiety disorders such as panic disorder, social anxiety disorder or post-traumatic stress disorder.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about the clinical relevance of overexpectation.

claim: The infralimbic cortex is considered to be the key brain locus in learning to downregulate fear responses.
source: The infralimbic cortex (IL) is considered to be the key brain locus in learning to downregulate fear responses (An et al., 2017; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Laurent and Westbrook, 2009; Lingawi et al., 2017; Milad and Quirk, 2002; Milad et al., 2004; Meyer and Bucci, 2014; Quirk et al., 2000; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2006; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Evidence for the role of the infralimbic cortex in fear reduction is exclusively derived from extinction designs.
source: Importantly, evidence for this role is exclusively derived from extinction designs.
evidence: This is an inference based on review of the literature.

claim: The lateral orbitofrontal cortex has dense reciprocal projections with the basolateral amygdala.
source: Firstly, it has dense reciprocal projections with the basolateral amygdala (Carmichael and Price, 1995; Price, 2007), which has been extensively implicated in fear acquisition and extinction (e.g., Davis, 2000; Courtin et al., 2014; Herry et al., 2008; Kim and Davis, 1993; Laurent et al., 2008; Orsini and Maren, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to anatomical studies.

claim: The basolateral amygdala has been extensively implicated in fear acquisition and extinction.
source: Firstly, it has dense reciprocal projections with the basolateral amygdala (Carmichael and Price, 1995; Price, 2007), which has been extensively implicated in fear acquisition and extinction (e.g., Davis, 2000; Courtin et al., 2014; Herry et al., 2008; Kim and Davis, 1993; Laurent et al., 2008; Orsini and Maren, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The lateral orbitofrontal cortex has been linked to fear and anxiety.
source: Secondly, the lOFC has been linked to fear (Zelinski et al., 2010; Asok et al., 2013; Trow et al., 2017; Chang et al., 2018; Ray et al., 2018; Zimmermann et al., 2018) and anxiety (Etkin and Wager, 2007; Milad and Rauch, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: The lateral orbitofrontal cortex supports learning from overexpectation of reward.
source: Finally, it supports learning from overexpectation of reward (Burke et al., 2009; Takahashi et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Fear conditioning was acquired to the tone and the light in Experiment 1.
source: Fear conditioning was acquired to the tone and the light (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1D and statistical analysis showing significant linear trend.

claim: There was no effect of training on fear conditioning to the tone in Experiment 1.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the conditioning data.

claim: The overexpectation-M/B and overexpectation-vehicle groups exhibited similar levels of responding to the compound stimulus during overexpectation training in Experiment 1.
source: The overexpectation-M/B and overexpectation-vehicle groups exhibited similar levels of responding to the compound stimulus during this phase (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1E and statistical analysis showing no effect of group.

claim: Rats trained in overexpectation with a functional or inactivated IL showed lower level of fear to the target cue compared to the controls in Experiment 1.
source: Rats trained in overexpectation with a functional or inactivated IL showed lower level of fear to the target cue compared to the controls (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1F and statistical analysis showing main effect of training.

claim: Infusion of M/B in the IL cortex prior to compound presentations during overexpectation training had no effect on retrieval of the overexpectation memory when tested drug-free.
source: These results indicate that infusion of M/B in the IL cortex prior to compound presentations during overexpectation training had no effect on retrieval of the overexpectation memory when tested drug-free.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis showing no training x drug interaction in the test phase.

claim: Rats infused with M/B in the IL showed higher levels of fear across extinction trials compared to rats infused with the vehicle in Experiment 1.
source: Rat infused with M/B in the IL showed higher levels of fear across extinction trials compared to rats infused with the vehicle (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2E and statistical analysis showing main effect of drug.

claim: Silencing the IL prior to extinction training disrupted subsequent retrieval of the extinction memory in Experiment 1.
source: Silencing the IL prior to extinction training disrupted subsequent retrieval of the extinction memory (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2F and statistical analysis showing training x drug interaction.

claim: Rats infused with M/B during extinction froze significantly more during presentations of the cue on Test compared to rats infused with vehicle in Experiment 1.
source: Post-hoc tests with Bonferroni adjustments revealed a significant difference within the extinction conditions: rats infused with M/B during extinction froze significantly more during presentations of the cue on Test compared to rats infused with vehicle (F(1, 33)=11.43, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.19, 1.52], d = 1.85); there was no effect of drug on the control condition (F(1, 33)=0.001, p=0.98, 95% CI [−0.82, 0.80]).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: IL function is necessary for supporting fear reduction driven by extinction but not overexpectation learning.
source: Taken together, these data provide key evidence for the dissociable role of the IL in fear reduction: IL function is necessary for supporting fear reduction driven by extinction but not overexpectation learning.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined results from Experiment 1.

claim: Inactivation of the lateral OFC prior to overexpectation training disrupted the overexpectation effect on Test in Experiment 2.
source: Inactivation of the lateral OFC prior to overexpectation training disrupted the overexpectation effect on Test (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 3F and statistical analysis showing training x drug interaction.

claim: Rats infused with vehicle prior to overexpectation training froze significantly less during presentations of the target stimulus on Test compared to the vehicle rats in the control condition in Experiment 2.
source: Post-hoc tests with Bonferroni adjustments showed that overexpectation training reduced fear to the target cue in rats with a functional lOFC: Rats infused with vehicle prior to overexpectation training froze significantly less during presentations of the target stimulus on Test compared to the vehicle rats in the control condition (F(1, 40)=5.93, p=0.019, 95% CI [−1.63, 0.06], d = 1.26).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: Rats trained in overexpectation and infused with M/B in the lOFC froze significantly more during presentations of the target stimulus at Test compared to the vehicle rats in Experiment 2.
source: This overexpectation effect was disrupted in rats trained under an inactivated lOFC: Rats trained in overexpectation and infused with M/B in the lOFC froze significantly more during presentations of the target stimulus at Test compared to the vehicle rats (F(1, 40)=10.93, p=0.002, 95% CI [0.21, 1.77], d = 1.44).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: In the absence of the lOFC, rats were not able to reduce conditioned fear responding that is driven by overexpectation training.
source: These results indicate that, in the absence of the lOFC, rats were not able to reduce conditioned fear responding that is driven by overexpectation training.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the results from Experiment 2 overexpectation phase.

claim: Infusion of M/B in the lOFC prior to extinction training had no effect on within-session performance in Experiment 2.
source: Infusion of M/B in the lOFC prior to extinction training had no effect on within-session performance (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4E and statistical analysis showing no main effect of drug.

claim: Overall, extinction training reduced fear on Test, but this extinction effect was not modulated by inactivation of the lOFC during extinction learning in Experiment 2.
source: Overall, extinction training reduced fear on Test, but this extinction effect was not modulated by inactivation of the lOFC during extinction learning (Figure 4F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4F and statistical analysis showing main effect of training but no training x drug interaction.

claim: The data provide clear evidence for a role of lOFC in fear reduction driven by overexpectation but not by extinction.
source: Taken together, these data provide clear evidence for a role of lOFC in fear reduction driven by overexpectation but not by extinction.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined results from Experiment 2.

claim: Extinction and overexpectation are dissociable in the cortex.
source: The results of Experiment 2 are important because they provide additional evidence to that presented in Experiment 1 that extinction and overexpectation are dissociable in the cortex (but see Iordanova et al., 2016 for evidence of convergence in the central nucleus of the amygdala).
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the combined results from Experiments 1 and 2, with citation to prior work.

claim: Inactivation of the lOFC disrupts extinction of fear.
source: However, our lack of an inactivation effect of the lOFC on extinction is somewhat at odds with previous studies showing that inactivation of this region disrupts extinction of fear (Zimmermann et al., 2018) and between-session extinction of reward associations (Panayi and Killcross, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Rats infused with M/B froze significantly more during presentations of the target stimulus at Test compared to vehicle rats in Experiment 3 initial extinction.
source: Post hoc tests with Bonferroni adjustments revealed that a significant difference within the extinction condition: rats infused with M/B froze significantly more during presentations of the target stimulus at Test compared to vehicle rats (F(1, 51)=4.51, p=0.039, 95% CI [−0.11, 1.15], d = 1.21); there was no effect of drug on the control condition (F(1, 51)=1.54, p=0.22, 95% CI [−0.39, 1.11]).
evidence: This claim is supported by post-hoc statistical analysis.

claim: lOFC inactivation during extinction resulted in a mild and not catastrophic impairment in the retrieval of the extinction memory.
source: These results are intriguing in that they reveal a disruption in extinction in animals trained with an inactivated lOFC. However, the data also show there is a clear effect of extinction in the inactivated animals relative to the controls, suggesting that lOFC inactivation during extinction resulted in a mild and not catastrophic impairment in the retrieval of the extinction memory.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the pattern of results in Experiment 3.

claim: Inactivation of the lOFC with M/B prior to extinction training had no effect on subsequent extinction learning in Experiment 3 re-extinction.
source: These findings confirm that inactivation of the lOFC with M/B prior to extinction training had no effect on subsequent extinction learning, replicating the findings of Experiment 2.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 3 re-extinction phase.

claim: The findings define the conditions under which the IL and the lOFC are recruited.
source: Our findings represent a fundamental contribution to the study of fear reduction because they define the conditions under which the IL and the lOFC are recruited.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results across all experiments.

claim: Inactivation of the IL during overexpectation learning left this effect intact.
source: Specifically, inactivation of the IL during overexpectation learning left this effect intact.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 1.

claim: Inactivation of the lOFC led to a catastrophic disruption of overexpectation but only a very mild, if any, actual impairment in extinction.
source: Inactivation of the lOFC, on the other hand, led to a catastrophic disruption of overexpectation but only a very mild, if any, actual impairment in extinction.
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: The data replicate substantial prior work from the aversive domain showing that inactivation of the IL during extinction training disrupts extinction retrieval on Test.
source: Our data replicate substantial prior work from the aversive domain showing that inactivation of the IL during extinction training disrupts extinction retrieval on Test (e.g., Quirk et al., 2000; Milad and Quirk, 2002; Milad et al., 2004; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2006; Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011; Laurent and Westbrook, 2009; Do-Monte et al., 2015; Lingawi et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by data from Experiment 1 and citations to prior research.

claim: The effect of IL inactivation on performance during extinction training has yielded variable results.
source: The effect of IL inactivation on performance during extinction training, however, has yielded variable results: Some studies show little to no effect on responding (e.g. Do-Monte et al., 2015), while others report a retardation (e.g., Sierra-Mercado et al., 2011) or facilitation (e.g., Mendoza et al., 2015; Lay et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research showing variable results.

claim: lOFC inactivation during extinction did not prevent animals from showing an extinction effect compared to the non-extinction controls.
source: lOFC inactivation during extinction did not prevent these animals from showing an extinction effect compared to the non-extinction controls and this difference was similar to that obtained from the vehicle animals.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the pattern of results in Experiment 3.

claim: Disrupting lOFC function did not abolish the ability to attenuate learned fear under extinction conditions.
source: This result is key because it shows that disrupting lOFC function did not abolish the ability to attenuate learned fear under extinction conditions.
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the pattern of results in Experiment 3.

claim: The lOFC has a very limited, if any, effect on extinction learning.
source: While these data provide evidence that the lOFC has a very limited, if any, effect on extinction learning, they must be taken with caution because we observed a substantial drop in performance at the outset of extinction training (Phase 2) seen in Figure 5 of Experiment 3 .
evidence: This claim is an inference based on the pattern of results in Experiments 2 and 3, with caution noted.

claim: The dissociation of function reported flies in the face of a parsimonious explanation for fear reduction in the IL and lOFC.
source: The dissociation of function reported here flies in the face of a parsimonious explanation for fear reduction in the IL and lOFC.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results.

claim: Both extinction and overexpectation methods are underpinned by the same negative prediction error mechanism.
source: Specifically, both methods are underpinned by the same negative prediction error mechanism (Rescorla and Wagner, 1972), which is generated when expectations surpass reality.
evidence: This is established knowledge from learning theory with citation.

claim: The IL and the lOFC are recruited under different task-dependent conditions to downregulate fear.
source: Instead, our findings suggest that the IL and the lOFC are recruited under different task-dependent conditions to downregulate fear.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results across all experiments.

claim: In extinction, the learning discrepancy results from omitting the delivery of an expected aversive event, which results in inhibition of fear responding.
source: In extinction, the learning discrepancy results from omitting the delivery of an expected (aversive) event, which results in inhibition of fear responding, and likely underlies the development of inhibitory cue-response associations.
evidence: This is an inference based on established knowledge about extinction and the current results.

claim: The pattern observed in the IL inactivation animals is consistent with inhibitory learning that likely involves cue-response associations.
source: Thus, the pattern observed in the IL inactivation animals is consistent with inhibitory learning that likely involves cue-response associations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results in Experiment 1.

claim: The role of the lOFC in overexpectation and its limited role in extinction suggest that the lOFC is unlikely to be involved in inhibitory learning involving cue-response associations.
source: In contrast, the role of the lOFC in overexpectation and its limited role in extinction suggest that the lOFC is unlikely to be involved in this form of inhibitory learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results in Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: In overexpectation the learning discrepancy depends on the summation of two individually trained associations with the aversive event.
source: Rather, in overexpectation the learning discrepancy depends on the summation of two individually trained associations with the aversive event, therefore the lOFC likely modulates fear reduction through cue-outcome inhibitory learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the nature of overexpectation and the current results.

claim: The lOFC likely modulates fear reduction through cue-outcome inhibitory learning.
source: Rather, in overexpectation the learning discrepancy depends on the summation of two individually trained associations with the aversive event, therefore the lOFC likely modulates fear reduction through cue-outcome inhibitory learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of results in Experiments 2 and 3.

claim: The dissociation of function between the IL and lOFC is in line with data implicating IL activation during reduction of conditioned fear using a habituation method.
source: Finally, the dissociation of function between the IL and lOFC is in line with data implicating IL activation during reduction of conditioned fear using a habituation method (Furlong et al., 2016), as well as research implicating the lOFC in cue-outcome associations (Lichtenberg et al., 2017; Zhang and Li, 2018, Takahashi et al., 2009, Asok et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Disruption of IL function interferes with appetitive extinction.
source: Disruption of IL function interferes with appetitive extinction (natural rewards: Rhodes and Killcross, 2004; Rhodes and Killcross, 2007a; Rhodes and Killcross, 2007b; Lay et al., 2019; drug rewards: Peters et al., 2008; LaLumiere et al., 2010; for review of IL in fear and addiction see Peters et al., 2008) but not with appetitive overexpectation (Lay et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The severity of the IL-dependent extinction deficit might be greater for the aversive relative to the appetitive case.
source: Notably, a comparison across experiments suggests that the severity of the IL-dependent extinction deficit might be greater for the aversive (Experiment 1) relative to the appetitive case (Lay et al., 2019).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of current results with prior research.

claim: The IL has a role in appetitive and aversive response inhibition.
source: Related to what may be learned in extinction, the IL has a role in appetitive and aversive response inhibition (Capuzzo and Floresco, 2020; Martínez-Rivera et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Electrophysiological and inactivation studies have linked the lOFC to appetitive overexpectation.
source: In regard to the lOFC, electrophysiological and inactivation studies have linked it to appetitive overexpectation (Takahashi et al., 2009), but not to response inhibition when a conditioned cue is followed by reward omission (Burke et al., 2009, see also Chudasama et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The lOFC fear data are in line with reports linking lOFC to appetitive overexpectation and join others in providing evidence that the lOFC has a role beyond the appetitive domain.
source: Our lOFC fear data are in line with these reports and join others (Asok et al., 2013; Baker et al., 2018; Chang et al., 2018; Ray et al., 2018; Sarlitto et al., 2018; Trow et al., 2017; Zimmermann et al., 2018) in providing evidence that the lOFC has a role beyond the appetitive domain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the current results and citations to prior research.

claim: The data circumscribe the role of the IL in fear reduction.
source: To conclude, our data circumscribe the role of the IL in fear reduction and identify the lOFC as a novel avenue for research and clinical intervention in fear-related disorders (but see Milad and Rauch, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results.

claim: The lOFC is identified as a novel avenue for research and clinical intervention in fear-related disorders.
source: To conclude, our data circumscribe the role of the IL in fear reduction and identify the lOFC as a novel avenue for research and clinical intervention in fear-related disorders (but see Milad and Rauch, 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results with citation to prior work.

claim: The data highlight the need to transcend the single-paradigm approach if a thorough understanding of the neural mechanisms supporting the reduction of conditioned responding is to be attained.
source: In addition, they highlight the need to transcend the single-paradigm approach if a thorough understanding of the neural mechanisms supporting the reduction of conditioned responding is to be attained.
evidence: This is an inference based on the overall pattern of results and the dual-paradigm approach used.

claim: One hundred and sixty-seven male Sprague Dawley rats weighing between 300–370 g were used across all experiments.
source: One hundred and sixty-seven (63 in Experiment 1, 48 in Experiment 2, 56 in Experiment 3) male Sprague Dawley rats weighing between 300–370 g were obtained from Harlan.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the subjects used in the study.

claim: Sample sizes were based on prior behavioural research in fear from the laboratory.
source: Sample sizes were based on prior behavioural research in fear from our laboratory (Mahmud et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a statement about the rationale for sample size with citation.

claim: Rats were implanted with bilateral guide cannulae in the IL or lOFC before behavioural training and testing.
source: Before behavioural training and testing, rats were implanted with bilateral guide cannulae in the IL or lOFC.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the surgical procedure.

claim: A cocktail of muscimol/baclofen or vehicle was infused bilaterally into the lOFC or IL.
source: A cocktail of muscimol/baclofen or vehicle was infused bilaterally into the lOFC or IL by inserting a 28-gauge injector cannula into each guide cannula.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the drug infusion procedure.

claim: A total volume of 0.3 µl was delivered to both sides at a rate of 0.1 µl/min.
source: A total volume of 0.3 µl was delivered to both sides at a rate of 0.1 µl/min, and drug delivery was monitored with the progression of an air bubble in the infusion tube.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the drug infusion parameters.

claim: Rats with incorrect placements or infection were excluded from the statistical analyses.
source: Rats with incorrect placements or infection were excluded from the statistical analyses.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the exclusion criteria.

claim: Fourteen rats were excluded from Experiment 1 based on incorrect placements or infection.
source: The numbers of rats excluded from each experiment based on incorrect placements or infection were fourteen in Experiment 1, three in Experiment 2, and one in Experiment 3.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the number of excluded subjects.

claim: Infusions of M/B outside of the IL cortex had no effect on the overexpectation effect.
source: The fourteen rats that were excluded from Experiment 1 were used as anatomical controls and infusions of M/B outside of the IL cortex had no effect on the overexpectation effect (F(1, 10)=0.63, p=0.45, 95% CI [−1.79, 1.01], mixed ANOVA) or extinction effect (F(1, 7)=2.41, p=0.16, 95% CI [−2.35, 0.79], mixed ANOVA).
evidence: This is a statement about anatomical control data with statistical analysis.

claim: Freezing was used to assess conditioned fear.
source: Freezing was used to assess conditioned fear. It was defined as the absence of all movements except those related to breathing (Blanchard and Blanchard, 1969; Fanselow, 1980) and exhibited a hunched posture.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the behavioral measure with citations.

claim: Each rat was observed every 2 s and scored as either freezing or not freezing by two observers, one of whom was blind to group assignment.
source: Each rat was observed every 2 s and scored as either freezing or not freezing by two observers, one of whom was blind to group assignment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the scoring procedure.

claim: The correlation between the scores of the two observers were high (Pearson r > 0.9).
source: The correlation between the scores were high (Pearson r > 0.9).
evidence: This is a statement about inter-rater reliability.
